transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-11-15 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Maria Gomez (CTO - Atlas Health), Ethan Park (ML Engineer), Sofia Ruiz (PM)

[00:00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Jordan from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. Priya's our solutions engineer, she'll run through the Optimize walkthrough. Maria, Ethan, Sofia, thanks for making time.
[00:00:12] Maria: Yeah thanks Jordan, excited to see the batching and cache stuff — latency and cost are both tight for us.
[00:00:18] Priya: Cool, quick agenda: we'll cover batching strategies, prefix/KV cache and hit-rate assumptions, then a simple cost model and recommended next steps. There might be a couple of slides, and I'll share a link to the benchmark sheet.
[00:00:30] Ethan: Awesome. For context, we're doing mostly clinical summarization and triage chats, average prompt length ~300 tokens, few long histories, throughput 200 rps at peak, but bursty.
[00:00:42] Jordan: Good context — bursty workloads usually push us towards dynamic batching + a small dedicated pool or burst capacity on Hosted. We'll dive in.
[00:00:55] Priya: Slide 1: Batching overview, uh we recommend continuous batching when latency SLO is 200-500ms, for tighter 50-150ms we use smaller max batch sizes and pref tsoins like early flush. Note: transcription may call it continous batching, it's continuous.
[00:01:17] Maria: We really need median <250ms and p95 <800ms. Is continuous batching compatible?
[00:01:22] Priya: Yes — with our runtime we do adaptive batching: we set a latency cap and the runtime forms batches up to a size or time cap. For example, with a 250ms cap you'll see small batches most of the time but higher throughput windows will auto-batch more efficiently.
[00:01:39] Ethan: What about KV cache? Our conversations include stable prefixes for a lot of prompts, could be 40-60% prefix reuse.
[00:01:46] Priya: That's ideal. We distinguish prefix caching (inline prompt prefixes, good for few-token cached contexts) vs KV cache (model key/value cache for autoregressie decoding). For Atlas use-case both help: prefix caching avoids re-encoding the same system+user preamble, KV cache saves decoder steps across repeated continuations.
[00:02:03] Sofia: Quick dumb question: how do we estimate hit-rate? Is there tooling?
[00:02:07] Jordan: We usually start with a conservative estimate from your telemetry — e.g. deduping prompt text, then run small replay to measure real hit-rate. Priya will share a script.
[00:02:17] Priya: Yep — I'll share a lightweight replay script and the benchmark spreadsheet link: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/atlas. The sheet has rows for hit-rate scenarios (20%, 40%, 60%, 80%) and impacts on tokens/server cost.
[00:02:30] Ethan: Great. Walk me through the cost model example.
[00:02:33] Priya: Simple model: cost_per_token * tokens_per_request * requests + baseline infra cost amortized. With caching: effective tokens_per_request = original_tokens * (1 - cache_hit_fraction) + tokens_for_cache_miss_overhead. For batching: batching improves throughput and lowers per-token compute due to kernel utilization; we model batching as X% improvement in token/sec depending on batch size and sequence length distribution.
[00:02:56] Maria: Can you give concrete numbers?
[00:02:59] Priya: Sure. Example from the sheet: baseline hosted with no cache, cost $0.00012/token, avg tokens 500 -> $0.06/request. With 50% prefix cache hit and 30% KV hit the effective tokens drop to ~260, cost/request ~ $0.031. Adding batching (observed 1.6x throughput gain at our test seq lengths) reduces per-token compute cost another ~20% in reserved pricing models. So net effect ~60% cost reduction in that ideal case.
[00:03:32] Ethan: Those are promising. Are the numbers sensitive to long tails? We have some conversations hitting 2k tokens.
[00:03:37] Priya: Yes, long sequences reduce batching efficiency and raise token costs — in the sheet we have a Long Tail tab. We recommend either route splitting (truncate + async long generation) or moving long-tail to a different model variant with higher throughput or quantization.
[00:03:52] Jordan: On Dedicated vs Hosted: Dedicated gives predictable throughput and better cost at scale but requires commit. Hosted is easiest to start, and our routing policies can fall back to cheaper model variants during spikes. For Atlas' regulatory needs, private deployment was mentioned earlier — that's a separate track (security deck).
[00:04:07] Maria: We will likely need VPC and KMS for keys. Also SOC2 and audit logs.
[00:04:12] Jordan: Yep, we'll share the security pack: https://redwood.example.com/sec-deck and a SOC2 summary.
[00:04:17] Priya: Back to caching: key knobs are TTL for prefix cache, max entries, and sharding strategy. For KV cache we size by average sequence length * KV size per token * hot sessions. For numbers: e.g., 500 token avg * 64 bytes per KV entry ~=32KB per session cached. If you have many simultaneous sessions that drives memory.
[00:04:41] Ethan: 64 bytes per k-v? I thought maybe 48 or 80 depending on model.
[00:04:45] Priya: yeah it's approximate, varies by quantization and model architecture; the spreadsheet has param sliders.
[00:04:52] Sofia: Operationally, what does cache invalidation look like for user context changes?
[00:04:56] Priya: On user-edit or context change you invalidate that user's prefix cache or KV cache namespace. We expose APIs to evict by key or namespace. Also provide metrics for hit/miss by namespace so you can tune TTLs.
[00:05:09] Jordan: Let's talk pilot: recommended 2-week pilot with sample traffic replay — measure hit-rate, latency p95, and cost delta. If results look good we discuss Dedicated sizing.
[00:05:19] Maria: Sounds good. We have a security review next week too — can we run both in parallel?
[00:05:23] Jordan: Absolutely, we can run the security packet review and pilot simultaneously.
[00:05:27] Ethan: On the runtime side, how do we handle bursty spikes? We can't have high p95 for patient triage.
[00:05:33] Priya: Two levers: autoscaling + burst capacity for Dedicated, or routing to lower-cost model variants for non-critical paths. There's also request prioritization and early-exit heuristics for very long tail.
[00:05:46] Maria: Any tradeoffs on quality when using KV cache? Do we risk stale context?
[00:05:50] Priya: If cache is used correctly it's transparent — KV cache holds decoder keys/values, it doesn't change model weights. Staleness only happens if you don't evict after context changes. For prefix caching you must ensure template tokens still apply. We'll show examples in the script.
[00:06:03] Jordan: Quick objection we hear a lot — security: are requests logged with PII? How long are logs retained?
[00:06:09] Priya: We support configurable retention, and you can opt out of logging specific fields. For Private/VPC you control retention and KMS. We'll share the retention matrix in the security deck.
[00:06:19] Sofia: Can you run through a short end-to-end example with numbers from our traffic?
[00:06:23] Priya: Sure — using Atlas sample: 200 rps peak, avg tokens 300, 40% prefix hit, 25% KV hit. Baseline cost/month estimate $XX,XXX. With caching and batching we model ~45% savings. I'll paste the exact calc into the benchmark sheet after the call — again sheet link: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/atlas.
[00:06:46] Ethan: Please include p95 latency projection for both hosted and dedicated.
[00:06:50] Priya: Will do.
[00:06:52] Jordan: Any other vendors in your evaluation?
[00:06:55] Maria: We're also talking to OpenAI for hosted, and evaluating Anthropic for quality, but the ops story is critical for us so Redwood's unified runtime is attractive.
[00:07:05] Jordan: Great to know.
[00:07:07] Priya: Ok final section: recommended initial config — start on Hosted with dynamic batching + prefix cache enabled, measure hit-rate, then move to Dedicated if commit makes sense. TTLs: prefix cache 24h to start, KV cache per-session TTL 1h, max entries tuned after pilot.
[00:07:27] Sofia: That seems reasonable. How long to spin up Dedicated pool?
[00:07:30] Jordan: If you commit, ~2-4 weeks for sizing and provisioning; pilot results will inform sizing.
[00:07:36] Maria: Let's recap actions and owners.
[00:07:40] Jordan: Recap: Jordan will send pricing and Dedicated vs Hosted doc; Priya will share scripts and benchmark sheet and KV sizing calc; Ethan will upload sample prompts and traffic; Atlas will confirm pilot start date and security contact.
[00:07:55] Maria: Confirming — security contact is me, Maria, I'll share SOC2 req doc.
[00:08:00] Jordan: Great. We'll schedule POC kickoff 2025-11-20 pending materials.
[00:08:06] Priya: I'll also include example configs for batching thresholds and an example of the early-flush param.
[00:08:12] Jordan: Thanks everyone. End notes: links will be in follow-up email: bench sheet, security deck, and a short writeup on caching best practices.
[00:08:22] Sofia: Thank you.
[00:45:00] [call ended]

Notes/Artifacts referenced: security deck (https://redwood.example.com/sec-deck), benchmark spreadsheet (https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/atlas), KV sizing script (will be shared), Dedicated vs Hosted one-pager. There were occasional transcription errors (model names, KV size bytes approximated).

Action items (text): Jordan to send pricing + dedicated vs hosted; Priya to share scripts, spreadsheet, KV sizing calc; Ethan to upload sample prompts; Atlas (Maria) to share security contact and SOC2 requirements.
